newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spot natgas surges on cold, pipeline cuts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spot natgas surges on cold, pipeline cuts.

text.p: U.S spot gas prices raced higher Friday, led by severely cold temperatures in the central U.S. and related pipeline supply restrictions, market sources said.
At the Chicago city-gate, prices jumped to as high as $6.50 per mmBtu early as traders learned that Northern Illinois Gas Co (NiGas) was limiting storage withdrawals through Monday.
However, shortly before nomination deadlines prices dipped to about $4.50, still almost a $1 over Thursday's level.
Along the Gulf Coast, prices began as high as $4.50 per mmBtu on Transco but then eroded into the $3.80s late.
On average, prices were up 30 cents to the $3.85-3.90 range.
Further east, New York city-gate prices gained at least 25 cents to the $4.50s as colder temperatures were forecast for the region this weekend and extending through early next week.
Similarly in the Appalachian region, prices jumped more than 20 cents to the high-$3.70s, lifted by the stronger Gulf values and the impending colder weather.
In the Midcontinent, where temperatures are hovering around zero, prices on average were up $1 to the $4.80-4.85 range, though deals were reported done anywhere from $6 early to $4.40 late.
The largest increase in price was at Demarcation, in Kansas, due to pipeline cuts on Northern Natural, traders said.
As a result of the cold-related cuts, prices surged into the $4.75-6.00 range.
Enron Corp, the parent company of Northern, was not available for comment.
In south Texas, where Houston temperatures dipped to a low of 32 degrees Fahrenheit, prices rose an average of 40 cents to the high-$3.90s.
Helping to relieve some supply tightness was Texas Utilities' return to full power of its 1,150 megawatt Comanche Peak 2 nuclear power unit, in Glen Rose, Texas.
In west Texas, Permian gas prices were up by about 50 cents to the low-$4 area.
As supplies tightened in the central U.S., some buyers went to the West Coast to meet demand in Texas and Oklahoma.
As a result, prices at the southern California border were at a discount to Permian in the mid-$3.80s, still up about 30 cents from Thursday.
